hero.eyebrow: Free course · No software to install
hero.title: Digital Literacy: learn by doing
hero.subtitle: Write documents, build spreadsheets and design presentations right in your browser. Stay safe online and use AI responsibly. Every step has practice and feedback.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can prepare a letter and résumé, track a budget with formulas, present your ideas clearly and protect your accounts.

outcomes.title: Understand computers
outcomes.text: Know the parts of a computer, how files and folders work, and how to keep things organised.

outcomes.title: Write professional documents
outcomes.text: Format letters, résumés and reports with headings, lists and tables.

outcomes.title: Work with data
outcomes.text: Use formulas such as SUM, AVERAGE and IF, sort and filter data, and turn it into charts.

outcomes.title: Present your ideas
outcomes.text: Build clear slide decks with readable text, good layouts and simple visuals.

outcomes.title: Use the internet well
outcomes.text: Read web addresses, search effectively and write clear emails.

outcomes.title: Stay safe online
outcomes.text: Spot scams, choose strong passwords and protect your privacy.

outcomes.title: Work in the cloud
outcomes.text: Store, share and collaborate on files from any device.

outcomes.title: Use AI responsibly
outcomes.text: Write good prompts, check AI answers and keep your own work honest.

assessment: Complete the required practice activities in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (60% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Finish the capstone, My Digital Portfolio, and review it against the checklist.
A finished course is verified by GrowQR and counts toward your Skill Passport.

faq.q: Do I need Microsoft Office or any software?
faq.a: No. The document editor, spreadsheet and slide studio run in your browser, so you can practise on any computer or a tablet. The lessons also explain the real programs so you can use them later.

If you are logged in as a student, your work is saved to your account when you press Check my work or Save. If you are not logged in, nothing is stored on our servers. You can always download what you made.

faq.q: What if I get something wrong?
faq.a: Nothing is lost. Each check tells you what is missing in plain words, offers a hint when you ask for one, and you can try again as many times as you like.
About 80 hours at your own pace. Most students finish one module a week with a few hours of practice.
No. It is optional and may not always be available. Every lesson, hint and check works without it.

activities.scenario: A computer works like a small factory: things go in, get worked on, come out, and are kept for later.

activities.title: Write a formal letter
activities.objective: Lay out a formal letter with a date, greeting, three paragraphs, a list and a closing.
activities.scenario: You are writing to your principal to ask for permission to organise a computer-skills workshop for Class 9 students.
steps: Type today's date at the top.
Start with 'Dear Principal,'.
Write three short paragraphs: why, when, and what you need.
Add a bulleted list of three things you need (for example room, projector, laptops).
Finish with 'Yours sincerely,' and your name, and make your name bold.

checks.label: A date at the top
checks.hint: Write the date like 12 March 2026.
checks.explain: A letter begins with the date so the reader knows when it was written.

checks.label: A greeting that starts with Dear
checks.hint: Type Dear, then the person's title.
checks.explain: A polite greeting such as 'Dear Principal,' shows respect.

checks.label: Three paragraphs of real sentences
checks.hint: Press Enter between paragraphs. Each should have at least 10 words.
checks.explain: Short paragraphs, each with one idea, make a letter easy to read.

checks.label: A bulleted list of at least 3 items
checks.hint: Use the bullet-list button, then press Enter between items.
checks.explain: A list makes a set of requests easy to scan.

checks.label: A polite closing
checks.hint: End with Yours sincerely or Yours faithfully.
checks.explain: Formal letters end with 'Yours sincerely,' followed by your name.

checks.label: Your name in bold
checks.hint: Select your name and press the B button.
checks.explain: Bold makes your name stand out as the signature.

activities.title: Format a school assignment
activities.objective: Use headings to give a document structure.
activities.scenario: Your teacher asked for a one-page assignment called 'Why Digital Skills Matter' with an introduction and two sections.
steps: Type the title and make it a Heading 1.
Add two section headings using Heading 2.
Write at least three paragraphs under them.
Underline one important phrase.

checks.label: A main title (Heading 1)
checks.hint: Choose Heading 1 from the style list.
checks.explain: A single title tells the reader what the document is about.

checks.label: Two section headings (Heading 2)
checks.hint: Put the cursor in the line and pick Heading 2.
checks.explain: Section headings break the text into easy parts.

checks.label: At least three paragraphs
checks.hint: Write 2 to 3 sentences in each paragraph.
checks.explain: Paragraphs group related sentences.

checks.label: One phrase underlined
checks.hint: Select a phrase and press U.
checks.explain: Use underline sparingly, for the single most important idea.

checks.label: At least 80 words
checks.hint: Add a few more sentences.
checks.explain: Aim for enough detail to explain your idea.

activities.title: Build your one-page résumé
activities.objective: Create a clean résumé with a centred name, section headings and a skills list.
activities.scenario: You are applying for your first part-time job. Make a one-page résumé an employer can scan in 10 seconds.
steps: Type your name at the top, make it bold and centre it.
Add an email address under your name.
Add headings for Skills, Education and Experience.
Under Skills, make a bulleted list of at least three skills.
Make one line a bit larger by changing its font size.

checks.label: Name centred
checks.hint: Click the line, then the centre-align button.
checks.explain: A centred name works as the heading of a résumé.

checks.label: Name in bold
checks.hint: Select the name and press B.
checks.explain: Bold draws the eye to the most important line.

checks.label: An email address
checks.hint: Type something like name@example.com.
checks.explain: Employers need a way to reach you.

checks.label: At least three headings
checks.hint: Use Heading 2 for Skills, Education and Experience.
checks.explain: Headings let a reader jump to what they need.

checks.label: A skills heading
checks.hint: Add a heading that says Skills.
checks.explain: A skills section is the quickest way to show what you can do.

checks.label: A bulleted list of three skills
checks.hint: Use the bullet-list button.
checks.explain: Bullets are easier to scan than a paragraph.

checks.label: A line with a different font size
checks.hint: Select a line and choose a size from the list.
checks.explain: A larger name stands out from the body text.

activities.title: Prepare a meeting notice
activities.objective: Design a short notice that gives people everything they need.
activities.scenario: Your club is holding a meeting. Write the notice for the school board.
steps: Type 'Notice of Meeting' as a bold, centred title.
Give the date, time and venue.
Add the word 'Agenda' and a numbered list of at least three topics.
Keep it under 120 words.

checks.label: A bold, centred title
checks.hint: Make the title bold and centre it.
checks.explain: A bold centred title shows what the page is.

checks.label: Some bold text
checks.hint: Select the title and press B.
checks.explain: Bold helps people see the title at a glance.

checks.label: Date, time and venue
checks.hint: Include the words Date, Time and Venue.
checks.explain: Readers need to know when and where to go.

spec.what: the words Date, Time and Venue

checks.label: An Agenda with a numbered list
checks.hint: Use the numbered-list button for the topics.
checks.explain: An agenda is a numbered list of what will be discussed.

checks.label: Under 120 words
checks.hint: Cut anything that is not needed.
checks.explain: A good notice is short.

activities.title: Write a short report with a table
activities.objective: Combine headings, paragraphs and a table in one report.
activities.scenario: You surveyed 3 classmates about the devices they use. Present the results in a short report.
steps: Add a Heading 1 title and two Heading 2 section headings.
Write at least two paragraphs that explain what you found.
Insert a table with at least 4 rows and 3 columns (a heading row plus 3 classmates).
Make the title a larger size.

checks.label: A title (Heading 1)
checks.hint: Choose Heading 1 for the title.
checks.explain: Every report needs a clear title.

checks.label: Two section headings
checks.hint: Use Heading 2 for the section headings.
checks.explain: Sections help readers find the results.

checks.label: Two paragraphs
checks.hint: Write at least 12 words in each.
checks.explain: Explain what the table shows in your own words.

checks.label: A table of at least 4 rows by 3 columns
checks.hint: Use the Table button and choose 4 rows and 3 columns.
checks.explain: Tables are best for comparing the same facts about several people.

checks.label: A larger title
checks.hint: Select the title and choose a bigger font size.
checks.explain: A larger title shows the importance of the heading.

activities.title: Your first spreadsheet
activities.objective: Enter data into cells and make the heading row stand out.
activities.scenario: A teacher wants a table of marks for four students in three subjects.
steps: Click a cell and type: names go in column A, marks in columns B to D.
Fill A2:A5 with four student names and B2:D5 with marks.
Make the headings in row 1 bold.

checks.label: Four student names in A2:A5
checks.hint: Click A2 and type a name, then press Enter to go down.
checks.explain: Each row is one student.

checks.label: Marks in B2:D5
checks.hint: Type numbers in the grid under the subject names.
checks.explain: Numbers are what formulas can calculate with.

checks.label: Heading row in bold
checks.hint: Select A1 and press B; do the same for the other headings.
checks.explain: Bold headings tell you which cells are labels.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: If a cell shows #VALUE!, check that marks are numbers.
checks.explain: Errors mean something in the sheet cannot be calculated.

activities.title: Calculate total and average
activities.objective: Use SUM and AVERAGE to calculate each student's total and average marks.
activities.scenario: Marks are entered. Work out each student's total (column E) and average (column F).
steps: Click E2 and type =SUM(B2:D2), then press Enter.
Do the same for E3, E4 and E5, changing the row number.
Click F2 and type =AVERAGE(B2:D2).
Fill in F3 to F5 the same way.

checks.label: E2 adds Asha's three marks with SUM
checks.hint: Type =SUM(B2:D2). The range B2:D2 means 'from B2 to D2'.
checks.explain: =SUM(B2:D2) adds every number from B2 to D2: 72 + 65 + 80 = 217.

checks.label: E5 adds Dev's marks with SUM
checks.hint: Change the row number to 5.

checks.label: F2 averages Asha's marks with AVERAGE
checks.hint: Type =AVERAGE(B2:D2).
checks.explain: =AVERAGE(B2:D2) is the total divided by 3: about 72.33.

checks.label: F5 averages Dev's marks
checks.hint: Use the same idea with row 5.
checks.explain: =AVERAGE(B5:D5) is 127 divided by 3: about 42.33.

checks.label: No error messages anywhere
checks.hint: Read the red message to see what is wrong.
checks.explain: A formula error always has a reason: a missing bracket, a wrong name or text instead of numbers.

activities.title: Personal monthly budget
activities.objective: Total your spending, find your balance and show whether you stayed within budget.
activities.scenario: Your monthly pocket money is ₹25,000 in this practice budget. Work out what is left after your expenses.
steps: In B9 total the expenses with =SUM(B3:B7).
In B10 work out the balance: income minus total expenses (=B2-B9).
In B11 type =IF(B10>=0,"Within budget","Overspent").
Format B9 as currency.

checks.label: B9 totals the expenses with SUM
checks.hint: Add B3 to B7 only, not the income in B2.

checks.label: B10 shows income minus expenses
checks.hint: Subtract the total in B9 from the income in B2.

checks.label: B11 uses IF to show the status
checks.hint: IF(test, if true, if false). Test whether B10>=0.
checks.explain: =IF(B10>=0,"Within budget","Overspent") shows Within budget while the balance is not negative.

checks.label: B9 formatted as currency
checks.hint: Select B9 and choose the currency format in the toolbar.
checks.explain: Formatting shows the ₹ sign and two decimals without changing the value.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: Check brackets and commas.
checks.explain: Each opening bracket needs a closing bracket.

activities.title: Student result analysis
activities.objective: Use IF, AVERAGE, MAX and COUNTIF to analyse a set of results.
activities.scenario: A class of six students sat a test. The pass mark is 40. Find out who passed and summarise the class.
steps: In C2 type =IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail") and fill C3 to C7 the same way.
In B9 find the average mark with AVERAGE.
In B10 find the highest mark with MAX.
In B11 count the passes with =COUNTIF(C2:C7,"Pass").

checks.label: C2 uses IF and shows Pass for 72
checks.hint: Test whether B2 is 40 or more.
checks.explain: 72 is at least 40, so =IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail") shows Pass.

checks.label: C3 shows Fail for 35
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 3 with B3.
checks.explain: 35 is below 40, so the result is Fail.

checks.label: C5 shows Pass for exactly 40
checks.hint: The pass mark is 40 or more, so use >=.
checks.explain: 40 >= 40 is true, so a student on exactly 40 passes.

checks.label: C7 shows Fail for 28
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 7.
checks.explain: 28 is below 40, so the result is Fail.

checks.label: B9 is the average of all six marks
checks.hint: Use AVERAGE over B2:B7.
checks.explain: =AVERAGE(B2:B7) is 321 divided by 6 = 53.5.

checks.label: B10 is the highest mark
checks.hint: Use MAX over the marks.
checks.explain: =MAX(B2:B7) is 91.

checks.label: B11 counts the students who passed
checks.hint: COUNTIF(range, "Pass") counts cells that say Pass.
checks.explain: =COUNTIF(C2:C7,"Pass") counts Asha, Meena, Dev and Priya: 4.

activities.title: Turn data into a chart
activities.objective: Choose a chart that shows a pattern and read it.
activities.scenario: A shop recorded its sales for six months. A chart will show the pattern faster than a table.
steps: Click the Chart button.
Choose a bar chart, labels A2:A7 and values B2:B7.
Look at the chart. In D2 type the month with the highest sales.

checks.label: A bar chart of the sales
checks.hint: Use labels A2:A7 and values B2:B7.
checks.explain: A bar chart compares amounts for each month side by side.

checks.label: D2 names the best month
checks.hint: Look for the tallest bar.
checks.explain: March had the highest sales (22,000), so the answer is Mar.

activities.title: Sort and filter a dataset
activities.objective: Sort data to answer a question and use a filter to focus on part of it.
activities.scenario: A quiz ended. The results are in the order students handed in their sheets. Find the top scorer.
steps: Click the Sort button and sort column B from highest to lowest.
Optionally try the Filter to show only marks of 50 or more, then clear it.
In D2 type the name of the top scorer.

checks.label: Marks sorted from highest to lowest
checks.hint: Use Sort on column B, largest first.
checks.explain: Sorting puts the biggest number at the top so the winner is easy to see.

checks.label: D2 names the top scorer
checks.hint: Look at the first row after sorting.
checks.explain: Meena scored 91, the highest mark.

activities.title: Introduce yourself in five slides
activities.objective: Build a simple, readable deck about yourself.
activities.scenario: Your class is meeting new people. Make five short slides so they can get to know you.
steps: Make slide 1 a Title slide with your name.
Add four more slides titled My Family, My Hobbies, My Goals and Thank You.
Write two or three short bullet points on each (one idea per line).
Choose a theme.

checks.label: Five to seven slides
checks.hint: Use Add slide to make more.
checks.explain: Five slides is enough to introduce yourself without losing people.

checks.label: A title slide first
checks.hint: Choose the Title slide layout for slide 1 and type your name.
checks.explain: The first slide introduces the talk.

checks.label: Every slide has a title
checks.hint: Type a title at the top of each slide.
checks.explain: Titles tell the audience what each slide is about.

checks.label: A slide about your hobbies
checks.hint: Make one slide's title or text include 'Hobbies'.
checks.explain: Hobbies and goals give the audience something to connect with.

checks.label: A slide about your goals
checks.hint: Make one slide's title or text include 'Goals'.
checks.explain: Goals tell people where you are heading.

checks.label: Few words per slide
checks.hint: Keep to 5 bullets and about 40 words.
checks.explain: Slides support what you say; they are not a script.

activities.title: A school project presentation
activities.objective: Design a consistent deck that is clear and varied.
activities.scenario: You are presenting a school project about 'Our Local Environment' to the class.
steps: Create 5 to 8 slides with titles.
Use at least three different layouts.
Pick a theme other than the default.
Add at least one shape to make a slide more visual.
Keep the text short on each slide.

checks.label: Five to eight slides
checks.hint: Use Add slide.
checks.explain: Enough to tell a story without rushing.

checks.label: Every slide has a title
checks.hint: Check each slide.
checks.explain: Titles help people follow along.

checks.label: At least three different layouts
checks.hint: Try Two columns or Section heading.
checks.explain: Variety keeps the audience interested.

checks.label: A non-default theme
checks.hint: Choose Ocean, Forest or Slate.
checks.explain: A consistent theme makes the whole deck look planned.

checks.label: At least one shape
checks.hint: Use the Shape button.
checks.explain: Simple shapes can show an idea or highlight a point.

checks.label: Short, readable text
checks.hint: Max 5 bullets and about 35 words.
checks.explain: If people are reading, they are not listening.

activities.title: Explain the water cycle
activities.objective: Explain a process step by step with a few simple visuals.
activities.scenario: Explain to Class 6 how water moves between the ground, the sky and back again.
steps: Make a slide for each stage: evaporation, condensation, precipitation.
Add shapes (for example arrows) between ideas.
Keep each slide to a few words.

checks.label: At least four slides
checks.hint: One slide per stage plus a title.
checks.explain: A process is easiest to learn one step at a time.

checks.label: A slide about evaporation
checks.hint: Include the word Evaporation.
checks.explain: Evaporation is water turning into vapour.

checks.label: A slide about condensation
checks.hint: Include the word Condensation.
checks.explain: Condensation is vapour cooling into clouds.

checks.label: A slide about precipitation
checks.hint: Include the word Precipitation.
checks.explain: Precipitation is rain, snow or hail falling.

checks.label: At least two shapes (such as arrows)
checks.hint: Use the Shape button; choose Arrow.
checks.explain: Arrows show the direction of the process.

checks.label: Every slide has a title
checks.hint: Check each slide.
checks.explain: Titles keep the story easy to follow.

Use at least three layouts and a theme.

checks.hint: Use Add slide.

checks.label: Covers phishing
checks.hint: Include a slide about phishing.
checks.explain: Phishing messages try to trick you into giving information away.

checks.label: At least three layouts
checks.hint: Mix layouts.
checks.explain: Variety helps the audience stay engaged.

checks.label: A non-default theme

checks.explain: A theme gives consistent colours and fonts.

activities.title: Read a web address
activities.objective: Know the three parts of a web address: protocol, domain and path.

steps: Read each piece of an address.
Say whether it is the protocol (how to connect), the domain (which website) or the path (which page).

It leads to one page, 'today', inside the news section.

activities.title: Spot the scam
activities.objective: Recognise the warning signs of phishing and online scams.
activities.scenario: Every day people receive messages that try to trick them into giving away money or passwords. Decide which of these to trust.
steps: Read each situation carefully.

items.text: An email from 'sbi-secure-alert@gmail.com' says your account will be blocked in 1 hour unless you click a link and enter your password.
items.why: Banks do not use free email addresses, and fake urgency is a classic trick.

items.text: A friend texts about tomorrow's meeting time, and it matches the conversation you had yesterday.
items.why: It fits what you already know and asks for nothing risky.

items.text: A pop-up says 'You won ₹50,00,000! Pay ₹500 to claim your prize.'
items.why: Real prizes never ask you to pay first.

items.text: Your school's newsletter arrives from its official address, and the links go to the school website you recognise.
items.why: The sender and the links both match what you expect.

items.text: A shopping website's address is written paypa1-login.com (with the number 1).
items.why: A look-alike address copies a real one with a small change.

items.text: An app asks for camera permission so it can scan a QR code you opened on purpose.
items.why: The permission matches what you asked the app to do.

activities.title: Responsible or risky use of AI?
activities.objective: Use AI to learn and save time without cheating yourself or sharing private information.
activities.scenario: AI is a powerful helper, but you are responsible for what you do with its answers.
steps: Read each situation.
Ask: is it honest, private and checked?
Sort it as responsible or risky.

items.text: Asking an AI to explain a topic, then checking it in your textbook.
items.why: You used AI to learn and then verified the facts.

items.text: Copying an AI-written essay and handing it in as your own work.
items.why: It is dishonest and you learn nothing.

items.text: Pasting your Aadhaar number into a chatbot to 'fill a form'.
items.why: Never share ID numbers, passwords or other private data with a chatbot.

items.text: Asking AI for better wording, then rewriting it in your own voice.
items.why: You stay in control and the work is still yours.

items.text: Following an AI's medicine dose without asking a doctor or pharmacist.
items.why: AI can be confidently wrong, and health mistakes are serious.

items.text: Turning your rough notes into a study plan that you review and adjust.
items.why: AI saves effort, and you check the result.
